players.product: 800G/1.6T PAM4 ICs, 200G/lane photodetectors, TIAs/drivers, CW lasers (developing) for optical modules

quarterly_data.signal: Fiscal Q1 2026 results: revenue was $271.6 million, up 4% sequentially and up 24.5% year-over-year, driven by growth across all three end markets. Adjusted gross profit was $156.5 million or 57.6% of revenue. Adjusted operating income was another record at $74 million, up 10.4% sequentially and up 33.5% year-over-year. Adjusted operating expense was $82.5 million (R&D $55.8 million, SG&A $26.7 million). Adjusted EPS was $1.02 on 76.7 million shares versus $0.94 in fiscal Q4 2025 - CFO Jack Kober called exceeding $1 per share of quarterly EPS a milestone. US domestic customers were approximately 45.6% of revenue.
quarterly_data.figure: Q1 revenue $271.6 million (up 4% sequentially, up 24.5% year-over-year); adjusted gross margin 57.6%; adjusted operating income $74 million; adjusted EPS $1.02

quarterly_data.signal: Q1 end-market revenue: Industrial and Defense $117.7 million (up 2% sequentially), Data Center $85.8 million (up approximately 8% sequentially) and Telecom $68.1 million (up 3% sequentially); Industrial and Defense and Data Center were both at record levels. Book-to-bill rose to 1.3 to one - one of the strongest quarterly bookings in the company's history and the highest quarterly book-to-bill since Q3 2021 - and CFO Jack Kober said MACOM saw 'a fair amount of strength' in Data Center book-to-bill (end-market book-to-bill not broken out). Orders booked and shipped within the quarter were 23% of revenue, higher than recent quarters because of strong early-quarter bookings, and backlog remains at record levels.
quarterly_data.figure: Data Center $85.8 million (up approximately 8% sequentially); Industrial and Defense $117.7 million; Telecom $68.1 million; book-to-bill 1.3 to one; turns 23% of revenue

quarterly_data.signal: Fiscal Q2 2026 guidance (quarter ending April 3, 2026): revenue of $281 to $289 million, adjusted gross margin of 57 to 59%, and adjusted EPS between $1.05 and $1.09 on 77.7 million fully diluted shares. By segment, Data Center is expected to grow low to mid-teens sequentially, and Telecom and Industrial and Defense low single-digit sequentially. Management expects sequential quarterly gross margin improvement of 25 to 50 basis points through the rest of fiscal 2026 (volume increases and new product introductions, net of cost increases such as gold and other precious metals). Full-year color (MACOM does not give full-year guidance): after 32% company growth last year, Telecom (which grew over 40% last year) is 'more likely going to be high single-digit, maybe low double-digit' - later 'thinking below 10% is a good way to think about it today' - and Industrial and Defense (close to 20% last year) is probably somewhere between 15-20%; internal targets put the company 'somewhere in the 20% range, plus or minus'. Q2 cash flow from operations is expected in excess of $60 million.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 guide $281 to $289 million; adjusted gross margin 57 to 59%; adjusted EPS between $1.05 and $1.09; gross margin +25 to 50 basis points per quarter; company growth in the 20% range (internal target)

quarterly_data.signal: MACOM raised its fiscal 2026 Data Center year-over-year revenue growth base case from 20% to 35 to 40%, with upside that is 'a bit unquantifiable right now'. CEO Stephen Daly said 'the key underlying driver is 1.6T', where MACOM sees the most design wins transitioning into production runs; the Data Center backlog is very healthy and the second half should be stronger than the first half in absolute revenue dollars. Growth is primarily in pluggable optical modules and optical cables using its 800G and 1.6T PAM4 products (supporting DSP, LPO and LRO module architectures, plus coherent DCI including ZR and ZR Lite), and hyperscaler capital investments are robust. A significant portion of Data Center revenue is 400 gig and above with 1.6T the fastest-growing portion; 'The real action is at 200 gig per lane PAM4' and next-generation coherent, while 25 gig per lane NRZ is holding up, 50 gig per lane PAM4 is flat and 100 gig per lane PAM4 is solid. MACOM supports all of the US hyperscalers as well as international hyperscalers, selling to builders of modules, AOCs and cables. Management does not frame the growth as share gain: 'I think the market's growing. We're winning designs.' The product roadmap extends to 3.2T.
quarterly_data.figure: Data Center FY2026 growth base case raised from 20% to 35 to 40%

quarterly_data.signal: LPO, LRO and copper: MACOM now has three hyperscalers embracing LPO and is 'in various phases of production' with them - in all cases 100 gig per lane for generally 800 gig modules; management expects LPO to remain a small part of the market for the next one to two years and to evolve into NPO/CPO/XPO. Customers are also investigating LRO at 1.6T using 200 gig per lane chips, and management sees LRO as more likely to happen first than 1.6T LPO. LPO interest is also appearing in PCIe, NPO and telecom front haul. On copper, there is renewed interest in MACOM's linear equalizers to extend active copper cable (ACC) reach at 800G and 1.6T and for backplanes (eliminating retimers, and important at 400 gig per lane), but Q1 contained no ACC revenue; management sees the ACC opportunity as bigger than backplane equalizers, and some customers are evaluating converting AECs to ACCs. MACOM launched a PCIe 6 optical chipset supporting sideband data streams over fiber and a new PCIe 7 equalizer, giving it new exposure to the compute side of the data center network.
quarterly_data.figure: three hyperscalers in LPO production phases (100 gig per lane, 800 gig modules); no ACC revenue in Q1

quarterly_data.signal: Photonics and CPO/NPO: demand for MACOM's 200 gig per lane photodetectors (for 800G and 1.6T) continues to grow, with indications that demand will remain strong into calendar 2027; the indium phosphide photodetector business is growing rapidly, higher-speed photodetectors are in development, and EML lasers are in test. CW lasers: two customers - module makers, the first line of entry before a hyperscaler PCN process adds MACOM to the approved vendor list - have confirmed MACOM's 75-milliwatt CW lasers meet their requirements electrically for their silicon photonics solutions, followed by a qualification phase lasting 'some number of months' and a fab production-readiness review. CEO Stephen Daly called it 'a watershed moment because six months ago, we were not in a position where we had a compliant laser'; MACOM does not make 400-milliwatt class lasers and does not sell lasers into 1.6 applications today, so this would be share gain. The product set sold into CPO or NPO platforms is very similar to pluggables (drivers, TIAs, photodetectors and possibly lasers); these platforms are moving quickly to silicon photonics, putting heavy demand on CW laser and photodetector chips, with far more channels per chip, and some systems are moving to coherent light. MACOM's future products are increasingly optimized for CPO and NPO.
quarterly_data.figure: 75-milliwatt CW lasers: two customers confirmed requirements met electrically; 200 gig per lane photodetector demand strong into calendar 2027

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and supply: MACOM is adding indium phosphide photodetector manufacturing capacity to keep up with customers' forecasted demand (amount not disclosed for competitive reasons). The North Carolina (RTP) fab has 'a very aggressive plan to increase output by 30%', with some equipment bought and cycle-time reduction as the site's number one priority. Gross margin gains this year and next come mainly from higher utilization of the Massachusetts fab and to some degree the French fab, whose three-inch to six-inch wafer transition is targeted to be fully qualified and released to production by June 2026; one high-mix fab runs GaAs, GaN, silicon and indium phosphide. Benefits from insourcing IPDs and capacitors now bought from a third-party vendor will most likely come in 2027 and beyond. On supply, 'we are absolutely in ramp mode in various programs', and availability of indium phosphide and other exotic materials is a key focus; pricing is rational, and 'we're in an environment where there is scarcity in some areas'. Fiscal 2026 capex is still estimated at $50 million to $55 million (Q1 capex $12.9 million).
quarterly_data.figure: RTP fab plan to increase output by 30%; FY2026 capex $50 million to $55 million; Q1 capex $12.9 million

quarterly_data.signal: Telecom: MACOM's previously announced $55 million satellite contract (with the potential of an additional $25 million add-on) is planned to start production in 2026, delayed mainly by satellite system changes flowed down from the customer, which management views as positive because added functionality should bring new customers to the constellation. MACOM says it is engaged at some level with all of the major LEO constellations (microwave, optics, satellite-to-satellite, direct-to-device and ground stations), has multiple SATCOM LEO programs in design, and expects SATCOM to grow nicely into 2027. In 5G, one competitor is exiting the RF power GaN market; MACOM hired a team of experienced engineers and is sampling next-generation GaN4 products, but expects share gains to take one or two years with a flat RAN market in 2026. Cable TV is expected to be a modest contributor to fiscal 2026 telecom growth.
quarterly_data.figure: $55 million satellite contract (potential additional $25 million add-on); production planned to start in 2026

quarterly_data.signal: Balance sheet and capital: cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments were $768 million, with a net cash position of more than $268 million as of January 2, 2026. MACOM planned to retire its 2021 convertible notes in mid-March by paying $161 million of principal in cash (conversion premium in shares), leaving approximately $340 million of convertible notes maturing in December 2029; share buybacks are 'not something that we're contemplating'. Q1 cash flow from operations was approximately $42.9 million and inventories were $238.9 million. Longer term, CEO Stephen Daly said management doubled the company in about four years and now wants to 'double the size of this company and not take four years', executing a strategic plan 'that gets us to $2 billion with a reasonable CAGR'.
quarterly_data.figure: $768 million cash and short-term investments; net cash more than $268 million; $161 million 2021 convertible notes to be retired mid-March; strategic plan to $2 billion
